title: Receipt Rewind
covers: multiplying decimals by estimating first, multiplying as whole numbers, and counting total decimal places
cert: multiplying decimals and placing the decimal point accurately using estimation and place counts

intro.caption: Lesson 2-12 — multiply decimals. The prop-market register glitched and printed wild totals on Clip Squad's receipts! Estimate first, multiply, and count total decimal places to rewind the receipts.

balloons.t: We bought 4.5 meters of LED strip at $12.60 per meter. Why does this receipt say $567?!
Register glitch! Time for a Receipt Rewind — estimate first, then place the point!
Whoa! $567 for lights?! Or is it $5.67? Where does that dot even go?!
Estimate first! 4.5 is near 5 and $12.60 is near $13. Five times $13 is $65!

pages.caption: An estimate tells you which neighborhood the product belongs in, so a misplaced decimal point stands out right away.

balloons.t: Round the factors first. $5.67 and $567 are nowhere near $65!
Multiply as whole numbers, then count the TOTAL decimal places in BOTH factors!
Count from the right, drop the dot, and check it against our estimate!
Watch out when factors are less than 1! Trailing zeros still count before you place the dot!
So 25 × 4 = 100 needs THREE places from the right — giving 0.100, or 0.1!
Two more glitched lines on the receipt — plus one rule check so we never mix up adding and multiplying!
Rewind those totals and get our refund!
Every decimal point in its rightful spot, full refund secured, and Dex did NOT drop the lights!

win.caption: Multiply as whole numbers, count the total decimal places in both factors to place the point, and check with an estimate.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Estimate First
gates.prompt: Use whole-number estimation to catch misplaced decimal points before you even multiply.
hints: Conceptual: rounding both factors gives a quick ballpark so you know if the answer is near $5, $50, or $500.
Procedural: round each decimal to a nearby whole number and multiply.

items.q: Which estimate proves 4.5 × $12.60 cannot be $5.67 or $567?

options.t: About 5 × $13 = $65, so the answer must be near $65
About 5 + $13 = $18, so the cost is near $18
options.fb: Estimate a product by multiplying rounded factors, not adding them.

items.q: For 3.8 × $9.25, the whole-number digits are 38 × 925 = 35150. Using 4 × $9 = $36, what is the exact cost?

options.fb: $3.52 is way too small for nearly 4 meters at $9 each!
$351.50 is ten times too big for 4 × $9 = $36!
You forgot to place the decimal point!

gates.pass: Around $65 and $35.15! Estimation immediately catches wild receipt errors.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Multiply & Count Places
gates.prompt: Multiply as whole numbers, then count the total decimal places in both factors.
hints: Conceptual: tenths × tenths gives hundredths (2 places); tenths × hundredths gives thousandths (3 places).
Procedural: multiply without decimal points, add the decimal-place counts of both factors, and count that many places from the right.

fb.msg: 5.67 is way below our $65 estimate! 4.5 (1 place) + 12.6 (1 place) = 2 places: 56.70 = 56.7.
You forgot to place the decimal point! Count 1 + 1 = 2 places from the right.

items.fbDefault: Multiply 45 × 126 = 5670, then place the decimal point 2 places from the right.

fb.msg: Count BOTH factors: 3.2 has 1 place and 4.15 has 2 places — 3 places total, not 2!
Too far left! 3 × 4 = 12, so the answer must be near 12, not 1.3.
Place the decimal point 3 places from the right.

items.fbDefault: Multiply 32 × 415 = 13280, then count 1 + 2 = 3 places from the right.

gates.pass: $56.70 (not $567!) and 13.28! Receipt line 1 is officially rewound.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Tiny Decimals
gates.prompt: Place the decimal point carefully when multiplying decimals smaller than 1.
hints: Conceptual: multiplying two numbers less than 1 gives an even smaller product.
Procedural: keep trailing zeros (like in 25 × 4 = 100) while counting decimal places from the right, and drop them only AFTER placing the point.

steps: Count 2 + 1 = 3 places from the right (annex a leading 0): 0.090 = 0.09.

items.label: Total decimal places in 0.25 × 0.4 before dropping zeros:

fb.msg: 0.25 has 2 places, AND 0.4 has 1 place. Add them: 2 + 1 = 3.
Count the decimal places in BOTH factors (2 + 1).

items.fbDefault: Add the decimal places in 0.25 (2) and 0.4 (1).

fb.msg: Count 3 places from the right in 100 (before dropping zeros): 0.100 = 0.1!
That's 4 places from the right. 0.25 × 0.4 has 2 + 1 = 3 places.
Multiplying two numbers smaller than 1 gives a result smaller than 1!

items.fbDefault: Multiply 25 × 4 = 100, then move 3 places from the right: 0.100 = 0.1.

gates.pass: 3 places and 0.1! Keeping the zeros while counting saves the day.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Audit the Receipt
gates.prompt: Fix the last two receipt lines and lock in how multiplying decimals differs from adding.
hints: Conceptual: multiplying by less than 1 makes the result smaller; multiplying counts total decimal places instead of lining up points.
Procedural: multiply digits, add the decimal places of both factors, place the dot from the right, and check with an estimate.

items.label: Lock 1 · 2.5 packs of batteries at $4.64 each (2.5 × 4.64):

fb.msg: Check your estimate (2 × $5 = $10)! Count 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places.
Too small for 2.5 × $4.64! Count 3 places from the right in 11600.

items.label: Lock 2 · 0.75 kg of prop glitter at $8.40/kg (0.75 × 8.4):

fb.msg: 0.75 kg is LESS than 1 kg, so it must cost LESS than $8.40!
Too small! 0.75 is three-quarters of 1, so it should be near three-quarters of $8.40.

items.q: Lock 3 · Why don't you line up the decimal points when multiplying decimals?

options.t: Because multiplying drops the decimal point forever
options.fb: You only multiply digits first — you MUST place the decimal point back in the product!

options.t: Because multiplying counts total decimal places in both factors instead of matching columns
Because multiplication always makes numbers bigger
Because decimal points only matter in addition
options.fb: Decimal placement matters just as much in multiplication!

gates.pass: $11.60, $6.30, and total decimal places mastered! The market cashier hands over the full refund!

journal.heading: Lesson 2-12 — what the receipt rewind taught us
rows: Round both factors to whole numbers so you know right away where the product belongs.
Multiply as whole numbers, then add the decimal places in BOTH factors to place the point from the right.
Count decimal places BEFORE dropping trailing zeros (25 × 4 = 100 → 3 places → 0.100 = 0.1).
Adding lines up decimal points; multiplying counts total decimal places.
journal.quote: "An estimate is a receipt's best friend." — Nova

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 2-12 (Multiply Decimals) as one focused read. Covers estimating products to catch misplaced decimal points, multiplying whole-number digits, counting total decimal places, and contrasting with decimal addition.
standards: Fluently multiply multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm
